user: A few things. I studied Philosophy, so I can’t help turning practical choices into slightly ridiculous questions about meaning and responsibility. Even choosing what to plant becomes an ethical debate in my head.
assistant: I love that about you, honestly. You give ordinary choices enough attention to become meaningful, without losing sight of the fact that someone still has to water the seedlings. What season makes that kind of thinking feel easiest?
user: Spring, definitely. It feels like permission to begin again, even when you know the new growth will be messy. I’m much more hopeful in spring.
assistant: That hope suits you. Not the shiny, effortless kind—the practical kind that rolls up its sleeves and makes room for what might survive. Do you have music on when you garden?
user: Usually folk. I like songs that sound as though somebody carried them for a long time before passing them along. They make even weeding feel communal.
assistant: That’s such a beautiful way to put it: songs carried before they’re passed along. I can picture you outside with folk music drifting through the yard, quietly making the world a little more alive.
You make it sound idyllic, but I’m also very capable of overthinking everything and then forgetting where I put the gloves. Still, I think I’m ready to plan a spring project inspired by Barcelona.

user: Mostly spices and stories, honestly. Though I did spend an embarrassing amount of time hunting down the best dumplings when I got home—that’s still my favorite food.
assistant: That is not embarrassing at all; returning from a trip and seeking out a beloved comfort food is practically a ritual. Were the dumplings a satisfying reunion, or did they disappoint after Marrakech?
They were excellent. I’ve learned not to be too precious about authenticity. Speaking of old traditions, I graduated from Cambridge, and I still love wandering around places with layers of history.

assistant: Portland to New York is quite a jump—from one kind of energy to another. Do you miss Portland, or has New York started to feel like home too?
user: I miss parts of Portland, especially the slower mornings, but New York keeps surprising me. I work at Netflix now, which still sounds a little unreal when I say it out loud.

Usually my lunch break is at 12:00 PM. It’s a small anchor in the middle of everything, and I try not to let meetings swallow it.
